title: On the Road to ‘Umrah, Quraysh’s Obstruction • The Pledge Under the Tree • The Terms of the Treaty, the Demand to Change the Name

blocks.0: On the Road to ‘Umrah, Quraysh’s Obstruction
blocks.1: The sixth year of the Hijrah. The Prophet {{1}} set out from Madinah with about fourteen hundred Companions, in ihram, with sacrificial animals along. One purpose only, the tawaf of the Ka‘bah, ‘umrah. A few days’ journey from Madinah. After stopping at a place by the road, news came that Quraysh had sent ahead a party of horsemen under Khalid ibn al-Walid. Khalid was not yet a Muslim. The Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.3: Khalid ibn al-Walid is at al-Ghamim with the cavalry vanguard of Quraysh. Take the right-hand road.{{1}}
blocks.4: Khalid did not even notice, until, seeing the dust of the Muslim army, he rushed to inform Quraysh. The army turned and descended into a mountain pass by which one can go down to the lower side of Makkah. Not wanting war, he had been avoiding the possibility of fighting. But to avoid it, if the road plan had to be changed, he changed it. The intention was peace, yet the eyes were open. The two go together.{{1}}
blocks.5: We often choose one of two directions. Either we walk with eyes closed in simple trust, or in suspicion we raise the sword at everyone. The Prophet {{1}} did neither. To avoid a quarrel, sometimes the very path must be turned; not meeting face to face is also an act of wisdom. As soon as they reached the pass leading down toward Makkah, the Prophet’s {{2}} she-camel Qaswa’ sat down and did not rise again. The people said, Qaswa’ has become stubborn. The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.7: Qaswa’ has not become stubborn, that is not her nature; she was held back by the One who held back the elephant. By the One in whose hand is my soul, whatever proposal they ask of me in which they honour the sanctities of Allah, I will give it to them.{{1}}
blocks.8: Though every reason for fighting was at hand, he decided beforehand: where the sanctity of what Allah has made sacred is protected, he would make concessions. For the one who holds power, making concessions is not weakness. News came that Quraysh were ready with weapons and would not let them enter the Ka‘bah. Envoys came and went. The Prophet {{1}} pitched his tent at the far end of Hudaybiyah, and repeatedly gave the same message, we have not come to fight, we have come to perform ‘umrah. At Hudaybiyah there was only one well. Fourteen hundred people and their camels, drawing water, until the well went completely dry, not a single drop remained. The news went to the Prophet {{2}}. Al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA) said,
blocks.10: He came and sat at the edge of the well. He asked for a vessel of water and made wudu’, rinsed his mouth, made du‘a, then poured the water into the well. We left the well alone for a little while. Then that well gave us and our mounts as much water as we needed.{{1}}
blocks.11: The enemy ahead, the road to the Ka‘bah closed, the well dry too. At the most helpless moment Allah showed that for the one with whom He is, no road is closed. And this same Companion used to say later, you count the conquest of Makkah as the conquest; we count as the conquest the Bay‘at al-Ridwan (the Pledge of Allah’s Pleasure) of the day of Hudaybiyah. The day that everyone then thought a defeat, for those who were there, that was the real victory. When we have nothing in hand we do the most reckoning, where will it come from, who will give. The Prophet {{1}} sat by the dry well. He used what he had: one vessel of water, wudu’, du‘a. Taking the tiny thing in one’s hand and raising the hands toward Allah.
blocks.12: The Comings and Goings of the Envoys
blocks.13: First came Budayl ibn Warqa’ of Khuza‘ah; he reported that Quraysh had gathered all their strength and would not let them enter the Ka‘bah. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.15: We have not come to fight anyone, we have come to perform ‘umrah. War has consumed Quraysh, wounded them badly. If they wish I will make a truce with them for a fixed term, they will leave me and the rest of the people alone. And if they refuse, then by the One in whose hand is my soul, I will fight them for this call of mine until my neck is severed.{{1}}
blocks.16: First the offer of peace, thinking of the enemy’s losses; but on the question of the call there is no compromise. Gentle words and an unshakeable decision, the two together. Then came ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud; what he said on seeing the Companions’ love has been told in dars one. Then came a chief of Banu Kinanah. The Prophet {{1}} said, this is a man of a tribe that honours sacrificial animals; take the animals before him. The line of animals garlanded around the neck passed before him, and the Companions welcomed him reciting the talbiyah. In astonishment he declared Allah’s glory and burst out, it is not right to turn these people away from the Ka‘bah. Going back he told Quraysh, I have seen the garlanded, marked animals; I do not think it right to hold these people back. No argument, no speech; only opening the purpose before the eyes. Speaking to each person in the language that person understands. Then came Mikraz ibn Hafs. Seeing him the Prophet {{2}} said, this is Mikraz, a wicked man. He came and began to speak.{{3}}
blocks.18: In the middle of the talks the Prophet {{1}} had sent ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan (RA) as an envoy to Makkah. He was delayed in returning, and a rumour spread that Quraysh had killed him.{{2}}
blocks.19: The Prophet {{1}} sat under a tree and took the pledge of the Companions. Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ (RA) was asked later, upon what did you pledge that day? He said, upon death. Jabir (RA) used to say, we were fourteen hundred; we pledged that we would not flee.{{2}}
blocks.20: The job of holding the branch aside was Ma‘qil ibn Yasar’s (RA); so that it would not touch the Prophet’s {{1}} head. ‘Umar (RA) was holding the Prophet’s {{2}} hand that day, Jabir (RA) said.{{3}}
blocks.21: His name is not written large in history. Yet the small task of holding a branch aside entered the picture of the pledge. We wait for a big task and leave the small one at hand lying. Yet the weight of a task is judged not by how small it is, but by for whom it is. Everyone pledged. Except one. Jadd ibn Qays al-Ansari hid with his head tucked under his camel’s belly.
blocks.23: We all pledged, except Jadd ibn Qays al-Ansari; he hid under the belly of his camel.{{1}}
blocks.24: One among fourteen hundred. Everyone stretched out their hands, he kept his head tucked down. If one in a crowd lags behind, the crowd loses nothing. But the picture of hiding at the call of duty in the end became his identity. And ‘Uthman (RA) was not there, in Makkah. Everyone pledged. Then the Prophet {{1}} placed one of his hands on the other and said, this is ‘Uthman’s hand. Ibn ‘Umar (RA) said later,
blocks.26: The Prophet {{1}}, with his right hand, said, this is ‘Uthman’s hand. Then, placing the left hand over it, he said, this is on behalf of ‘Uthman.{{2}}
blocks.27: The one who is not present, his share too he took for himself. Stretching out the hand on behalf of the absent is the Prophet’s {{1}} model. In our gatherings, who says a good word on behalf of one who is not there? In one’s mouth the word of death, in another’s the word of not fleeing; the aim is one, not to turn back before the enemy. The Qur’an has told of this pledge like this,
blocks.29: Surely Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts. So He sent down tranquility upon them and rewarded them with a nearby victory.{{1}}
blocks.30: The pledge taken for death, in its place Allah gave pleasure and the good news of a nearby victory; that victory was Khaybar, the very next year. ‘Uthman (RA) had not been killed; the rumour was false. But the worth of the pledge did not diminish. Allah saw the readiness of the heart, not the outcome. The Prophet {{1}} said later,
blocks.32: Allah willing, not one of those who pledged under the tree will enter the Fire.{{1}}
blocks.33: Often our preparation is tested with a danger that in the end does not come at all. Because the danger did not come, the preparation is not wasted; what gets written with Allah is that day’s intention alone. There is another thing about this tree. The next year the Companions returned by that road. Ibn ‘Umar (RA) said,
blocks.35: The next year we went back, but not even two men of us could agree on the tree under which we had pledged. It was a mercy from Allah.{{1}}
blocks.36: Which tree it was, no one could say for sure. Ibn ‘Umar (RA) called it Allah’s mercy. The place of the tree under which such a great event happened, forgotten; so that people remember not a tree but the pledge.
blocks.37: The Terms of the Treaty, the Demand to Change the Name
blocks.38: ‘Uthman (RA) returned safely. Now Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, to write the treaty. Seeing him coming the Prophet {{1}} said, your affair has now become easy. Even in the name there is a kind of good omen; Suhayl, ease. The writing began. The Prophet {{2}} said, write, Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Suhayl said, what is al-Rahman, I do not know; write, Bismika Allahumma, as you used to write before. The Muslims said, we will write only Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. The Prophet {{3}} said, write Bismika Allahumma. Then he said, write, this is the treaty that Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has made. Suhayl objected, if we knew you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have kept you from the Ka‘bah, nor fought you; write, Muhammad ibn ‘Abdillah. The Prophet {{4}} said,
blocks.40: By Allah, I am certainly the Messenger of Allah, even if you deny me. Write, Muhammad ibn ‘Abdillah.{{1}}
blocks.41: ‘Ali (RA) was writing then. He did not agree to erase the word ‘Rasul Allah’; the Prophet {{1}} told him to point out the place, then erased it with his own hand.{{2}}
blocks.42: The terms were finalised. This year they must go back without performing ‘umrah; next year they may come and stay three days. If anyone of Quraysh became Muslim and went to Madinah he must be returned; if anyone came from Madinah to Makkah Quraysh would not return him. And for ten years there would be no war between the two sides.{{1}}
blocks.43: Hearing the condition of returning, the Companions were stunned. They asked, O Messenger of Allah, shall we write this too? The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.45: Yes. Whoever of us goes to them, Allah Himself has removed him. And whoever of them comes to us, Allah will make for him a way of release.{{1}}
blocks.46: In the very condition that seemed the greatest loss, he placed two things. The one who leaves Islam and goes to them, we have no need of him. And the one who comes to us oppressed, Allah will open his way. How the condition later came undone has come in the story of Abu Basir. Another fruit of the treaty was in the enemy’s house too. The Qur’an has said it like this,
blocks.48: It is He who held their hands back from you and your hands back from them in the valley of Makkah, after He had given you the upper hand over them. Allah was seeing all that you were doing.{{1}}
blocks.49: A group of people of Makkah had come down with weapons, to attack the Prophet {{1}} and the Companions if they got the chance. They were caught. The Muslims had full power in their hands. Yet Allah so set the minds that no hand was raised. They were released. Releasing after having them in hand. The Qur’an calls this Allah’s own doing. When we get the chance we settle accounts; at home, at the office, in dealings. Releasing an opponent who has come into one’s hands is not an easy task.{{2}}
blocks.50: Agreeing to change the name, erasing a word; in none of this was there any lack of faith. What is written on paper does not change prophethood. Where conceding keeps the real thing intact, insisting on words is rather the path of losing something big. Whose obstinacy it was that day, and whose patience; the Qur’an has told it like this,
blocks.52: When those who disbelieved set in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Jahiliyyah, then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and the Muslims, and kept them firmly on the word of taqwa; and they were indeed the more deserving of it and worthy of it. Allah is All-Knowing of everything.{{1}}
blocks.53: Objection to the word ‘Rahman’, objection to the word ‘Rasul Allah’; on one side Jahili pride. On the other, tranquility, which Allah Himself sent down. Keeping a cool head in a moment that feels humiliating is not weakness; it is the sakinah given by Allah. From outside the treaty looked one-sided. Inside it was the opposite. For the first time Quraysh sat at the treaty table with the Muslims, as equals. Until then they had counted the Muslims as the dust of the road; this time they had to write a treaty naming them. No war for ten years means for ten years no way to block the call. And the number that was fourteen hundred on the day of the treaty became ten thousand on the day of the conquest of Makkah.{{1}}
blocks.54: A treaty is to be measured not by looking at the paper of terms, but by looking at the result. Often the concession that feels like a loss comes back later as the greatest win.

footnotes.0: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (the beginning of the joint narration of al-Miswar and Marwan; in this edition of Bukhari 2748–2749, ‘Bab al-Shurut fi al-Jihad’, vol. 4, p. 566): ‘Khalid ibn al-Walid is at al-Ghamim with the cavalry vanguard of Quraysh; take the right-hand road’. ‘Ghamim’ is a place toward Makkah, ‘qatarah’ means dust. ‘Thaniyyah’ is the pass from which one goes down toward Makkah. Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 560–561 (the spies and Khalid’s horsemen).
footnotes.1: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731, 2732 (the long joint narration of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, the whole course of Hudaybiyah); the number fourteen hundred in Sahih al-Bukhari 4154 (from Jabir (RA)).
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (through al-Miswar and Marwan). The she-camel sat down in the pass (al-thaniyyah) descending toward Makkah, then he took position at the far end of Hudaybiyah.
footnotes.3: Sahih al-Bukhari 4150 (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA); at the beginning of the same hadith ‘you count the conquest of Makkah as the conquest, we count as the conquest the Bay‘at al-Ridwan of the day of Hudaybiyah’ and ‘we were fourteen hundred’). Ibn Hibban 4801; Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: sahih on the condition of al-Bukhari. In the narration of Jabir (RA) the incident of water gushing from between the Prophet’s {{1}} fingers is also at Hudaybiyah (Sahih al-Bukhari 3576, 4152).
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (through al-Miswar and Marwan; the Prophet’s {{1}} message to Budayl ibn Warqa’). The last sentence ‘la-uqatilannahum ‘ala amri hadha hatta tanfarida salifati’; ‘salifah’ is the side of the neck, meaning: until death. Al-Albani, Fiqh al-Sirah p. 324 has called this part sahih.
footnotes.5: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (the order of the envoys: Budayl, ‘Urwah, the man of Banu Kinanah, Mikraz, then Suhayl; the Kinani man’s ‘it is not right to turn these people away from the Ka‘bah’ and about Mikraz ‘rajulun fajir’). The name of the Kinani man is Hulays ibn ‘Alqamah, in Ibn Ishaq’s narration. The sending of ‘Uthman (RA) as envoy and the pledge were in the middle of this, before Suhayl (Ibn Ishaq).
footnotes.6: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Hudaybiyah’ (‘Uthman (RA) going as envoy and the rumour of his being killed). Sirah-based.
footnotes.7: Sahih al-Bukhari 4169 (Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ (RA): pledge upon death); Jabir (RA)’s pledge ‘upon not fleeing’ is in Kitab al-Imarah of Sahih Muslim. Scholars have reconciled the two as two sides of the same pledge.
footnotes.8: Sahih Muslim 1858 (from Ma‘qil ibn Yasar (RA): ‘I was holding a branch of the tree up away from the head of the Prophet {{1}}; we were fourteen hundred; we did not pledge to him upon death, we pledged upon not fleeing’). Ahmad 20293 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: sahih on the condition of Muslim). Sahih Muslim 1856 (Jabir (RA): ‘‘Umar was holding his hand; the tree was an acacia’). Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 560.
footnotes.9: Sahih Muslim 1856 (Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA): ‘we were fourteen hundred, we pledged to him, ‘Umar was holding his hand; we all pledged except Jadd ibn Qays al-Ansari, he was hiding under his camel’s belly’). Ahmad 15259 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: chain hasan). Calling Jadd a ‘hypocrite’ is the view of the Sirah and of some scholars; in the text of Sahih Muslim only ‘was hiding’. Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 560 (he was a hypocrite, in these words).
footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari 4066, 3698 (Ibn ‘Umar (RA): the reason for ‘Uthman (RA)’s absence from the pledge; ‘if there had been anyone in Makkah more honoured than ‘Uthman, he would have sent him’; the Prophet {{1}} said with his right hand, ‘this is ‘Uthman’s hand’, then placed his left hand on it and said, ‘this is on behalf of ‘Uthman’). Also in Ahmad 6011 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: sahih on the condition of the two Shaykhs).
footnotes.11: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah al-Fath 48:18, p. 373 (Taqi ‘Uthmani; checked against the rendered PDF). Note 15: the verse alludes to the Bay‘at al-Ridwan; they pledged with sincere firm resolve, not as false promisers like the hypocrites. Note 16: by ‘the nearby victory’ the conquest of Khaybar is meant.
footnotes.12: Sahih Muslim 2496 (through Jabir (RA), from Umm Mubashshir al-Ansariyyah (RA); said in the presence of Hafsah (RA)).
footnotes.13: Sahih al-Bukhari 2958 (Nafi‘, a freed slave of Ibn ‘Umar; Ibn ‘Umar (RA) said, ‘coming back the next year, not even two men of us could agree on the tree under which we had pledged; this was a mercy from Allah’). Ahmad 23676: Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyib says his father (al-Musayyib ibn Hazn) was there that year, ‘the next year we forgot the tree’ (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: sahih).
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (through al-Miswar and Marwan). The incident of writing ‘Bismika Allahumma’ is in this hadith too. The sentence on seeing Suhayl ‘your affair has become easy’ is in Bukhari 2731 through Ma‘mar ← Ayyub ← ‘Ikrimah (the mursal part); the good omen with the name is from the commentators.
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 2699 (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA); ‘Ali (RA)’s refusal to erase and the Prophet’s {{1}} erasing it with his own hand).
footnotes.16: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (the condition of returning, ‘umrah the next year); 2699 (the condition of staying three days the next year); the ten-year term appears in Sunan Abi Dawud 2766 and in Ibn Ishaq’s narration; in the original text of Sahih al-Bukhari there is no number of years.
footnotes.17: Sahih Muslim 1784 (from Anas ibn Malik (RA); the Companions’ question at the time of writing the condition ‘O Messenger of Allah, shall we write this?’ and the answer ‘Yes, whoever goes from us to them, Allah has removed him; and whoever comes from them to us, Allah will make a way of release for him’). Ahmad 13827 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: sahih on the condition of Muslim). Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 567 (the same sentence).
footnotes.18: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah al-Fath 48:24, p. 375 (read from the printed page).
footnotes.19: Sahih Muslim 1808 (from Anas ibn Malik (RA)): ‘Eighty of the people of Makkah came down from the mountain of Tan‘im with weapons, intending to attack the Prophet {{1}} and his Companions unawares; he seized them in peace (peacefully), spared them (let them go); then Allah revealed the verse.’ Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, 48:24, p. 375; note 22 (p. 375): while ‘Uthman (RA) was in Makkah fifty of Quraysh had come to carry out a secret attack, the Muslims caught them; Allah made the Muslims’ mood favour not killing the prisoners. (In number, ‘eighty’ in Muslim, ‘fifty’ in the Tawdih; the numbers of the two narrations have not been reconciled, so no number is given in the talk.)
footnotes.20: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah al-Fath 48:26, p. 377 (Taqi ‘Uthmani; checked against the rendered PDF). Note 27: the objection to writing Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim and Rasul Allah when writing the treaty was due to Jahili pride and self-conceit; the Companions were very angry, Allah gave them extra forbearance, that is the ‘sakinah’. Note 28: ‘the word of taqwa’ means obedience to Allah and the Messenger in all circumstances, however unpleasant.
footnotes.21: Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 565–568 (‘The Essence of the Treaty’; Quraysh’s recognition, the ten-year truce, the path of spreading Islam, the result: in just two years the number from three thousand to ten thousand). The figure is al-Rahiq’s calculation: ‘at some moments no more than three thousand, within just two years of the conquest of Makkah ten thousand’. Verse Tawbah 9:13 (‘they were the ones who first began the quarrel with you’), which al-Rahiq quotes.

quiz.q: When Qaswa’ sat down, the Prophet ﷺ said, she was held back by the One who held back whom?
quiz.e: ‘Habis al-Fil’, the One who held back the elephant.

quiz.q: To avoid Khalid ibn al-Walid’s horsemen, which road did the Prophet ﷺ tell them to take?
quiz.e: ‘Take the right-hand road’ (Sahih al-Bukhari 2731).

quiz.q: What does the incident of avoiding Khalid’s horsemen at al-Ghamim by taking the right-hand road teach?
o: With trust in Allah there is no need to choose a path
Fighting the enemy is always inevitable
With the intention of peace, caution goes too
quiz.e: The intention was peace, yet the eyes were open.

quiz.q: Changing the path on a hint of danger fits with which instruction?
o: Allah will bring out His way
quiz.e: Caution and the intention of peace together.

quiz.q: Speaking to each person in the language that person understands; which incident is the lesson of?
o: The chief of Kinanah and the animals
quiz.e: The purpose was opened before his eyes.

quiz.q: Who was sent as an envoy to Makkah, about whom the rumour of killing spread?
quiz.e: ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan (RA).

quiz.q: In the words of Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ (RA), upon what was the pledge made?
quiz.e: Salamah (RA) said, upon death.

quiz.q: How did the Prophet ﷺ take the pledge on behalf of ‘Uthman (RA)?
o: By sending a letter to Makkah
By calling his own right hand ‘Uthman’s hand
quiz.e: Raising his right hand he said, this is ‘Uthman’s hand.

quiz.q: Who held the branch of the tree away from above the Prophet’s ﷺ head on the day of the pledge?
quiz.e: Sahih Muslim 1858.

quiz.q: Who was hiding under the camel’s belly at the time of the pledge?
quiz.e: Sahih Muslim 1856 (Jabir (RA)).

quiz.q: Saying ‘this is ‘Uthman’s hand’, what did the Prophet ﷺ do?
o: Announced a separate pledge in ‘Uthman’s name
Placing the other hand above, took the pledge on ‘Uthman’s behalf
Left ‘Uthman off the list of the pledge
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 4066, 3698 (Ibn ‘Umar (RA)).

quiz.q: The next year, about the tree, what did Ibn ‘Umar (RA) say?
o: The tree had been cut down, so it could not be recognised
Everyone recognised the tree easily, so the pledge was taken again
A new pledge was taken again under the tree
Not even two men could agree; this was Allah’s mercy
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 2958.

quiz.q: Even after it became known that ‘Uthman (RA) had not been killed, why did the worth of the pledge not diminish?
o: Allah gives value to the readiness of the heart
Another pledge was taken anew later
The rumour was in fact true
quiz.e: The verse says: Allah knew what was in their hearts.

quiz.q: In placing his hand on ‘Uthman’s (RA) behalf, what distinction of his is revealed?
o: He had failed in the duty of envoy
He had been left out of the pledge
Included in the pledge even while absent
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ called his own hand ‘Uthman’s hand.

quiz.q: How do Salamah’s (RA) ‘upon death’ and Ma‘qil’s and Jabir’s ‘upon not fleeing’ narrations fit together?
o: Two sides of the same pledge
One only of the Muhajirun, the other of the Ansar
quiz.e: Scholars’ reconciliation: the pledge not to flee is itself the preparation for death.

quiz.q: In the incident of ‘this is ‘Uthman’s hand’, what model of the Prophet ﷺ is caught?
o: Remembering the share of the absent too
Taking all decisions with his own hand
quiz.e: The share of the one not present, the Prophet ﷺ himself took.

quiz.q: A colleague at work deliberately avoided a meeting and hid; which picture of the pledge fits with this?
quiz.e: Everyone stretched out hands, he kept his head tucked down (Muslim 1856).

quiz.q: In place of ‘Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim’, what did Suhayl ask to be written?
quiz.e: He said, as you used to write before, Bismika Allahumma.

quiz.q: According to the treaty, how many days could they stay in Makkah the next year?
quiz.e: The condition was to stay three days the next year.

quiz.q: When did the Prophet ﷺ say ‘whoever of us goes to them, Allah Himself has removed him’?
o: While writing the condition of returning
quiz.e: Sahih Muslim 1784.

quiz.q: Why was there no harm to prophethood in erasing ‘Rasul Allah’ from the treaty?
o: The word was written again later
Suhayl acknowledged it with his mouth
The treaty never came into effect
Prophethood does not change by words on paper
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ himself said, I am the Messenger of Allah, even if you deny me.

quiz.q: What did the Tawdih al-Qur’an mean by ‘holding the hands back’ in Fath 48:24?
o: Not killing prisoners even with power
quiz.e: Note 22 (p. 375): Allah made the Muslims’ mood favour not killing the prisoners.

quiz.q: As a ‘result’ of the treaty, which matter does al-Rahiq al-Makhtum mention?
o: Madinah’s boundary growing up to Makkah
Followers from three to ten thousand
quiz.e: After the treaty in just two years the number grew to nearly ten thousand.

quiz.q: In a hard decision at the office, loss seems first and gain later; which matter does this fit?
quiz.e: A treaty is to be measured by the result, not by the terms.

quiz.q: The lesson of not taking revenge even after getting power is in the background of which verse?
quiz.e: Allah held back the hands, even after granting power.
